title: 1 Samuel 12:16–25
context: 1 Samuel 12:16–25 completes the address. Samuel calls for thunder and rain at wheat harvest, an unusual season for rain, as a sign that the people’s request for a king was evil. The people fear and ask Samuel to pray for them. Samuel tells them not to be afraid and not to turn aside after vain things, assures them that the LORD will not forsake his people for his great name’s sake, promises to keep praying and teaching, and warns that persistent evil will bring ruin on both people and king. Both traditions read the thunder as God’s witness, and both hold together God’s commitment to his people and the call to serve him faithfully, though they explain how those fit together differently.

verses.text: “Now therefore stand still and see this great thing, which the LORD will do before your eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel calls the people to stand still and see the great thing the LORD will do before their eyes. Arminians see God confirming the prophet’s message with a visible sign, so that the people cannot dismiss the warning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the echo of Exodus 14:13, where Israel is told to stand still and see the LORD’s salvation. Both traditions read the sign as God’s witness, shared ground in both traditions.

verses.text: Isn’t it wheat harvest today? I will call to the LORD, that he may send thunder and rain; and you will know and see that your wickedness is great, which you have done in the LORD’s sight, in asking for a king.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel notes it is wheat harvest and says he will call for thunder and rain so they will see that asking for a king was great wickedness. Arminians see the sign as unmistakable, since rain at wheat harvest was unusual in Israel’s climate, and as a call to recognize sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and observe that rain at harvest could damage crops, so the sign carries a note of judgment. Both traditions read the thunder as God’s witness against the request and as confirming Samuel’s word.

verses.text: So Samuel called to the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day. Then all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel calls to the LORD, who sends thunder and rain, and the people greatly fear the LORD and Samuel. Arminians see the people moved to fear by God’s direct response, which recalls Samuel’s earlier victory when the LORD thundered against the Philistines (7:10).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the sign as God vindicating his prophet. Both traditions see the fear as the right response to God’s power and holiness, and both note that it opens the way for repentance in the next verse.

verses.text: All the people said to Samuel, “Pray for your servants to the LORD your God, that we not die; for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for a king.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people ask Samuel to pray for them so they will not die, confessing that they added to their sins by asking for a king. Arminians see genuine conviction and confession, and they see the people seeking intercession as a right response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the people now confess what Samuel said in 12:17. Both traditions see the request for prayer as acknowledging their need for mercy and Samuel’s role as intercessor, like Moses before him.

verses.text: Samuel said to the people, “Don’t be afraid. You have indeed done all this evil; yet don’t turn away from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says, "Don’t be afraid," admits they have done evil, and urges them not to turn away from following the LORD but to serve him with all their heart. Arminians see grace meeting confession: the past sin does not cancel the call, but the people must now choose to keep following.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the comfort comes first, followed by the call. Both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s mercy does not leave his people in fear but calls them to wholehearted service. They differ, as in 12:14, on how that service relates to God’s enabling grace.

verses.text: Don’t turn away to go after vain things which can’t profit or deliver, for they are vain.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel warns against turning to vain things that cannot profit or deliver. Arminians see the warning as a real danger, since Israel’s history shows that God’s people can be drawn to idols, which can never give what they promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The word for "vain things" is used elsewhere for idols and emptiness. Both traditions read the verse as contrasting powerless idols with the LORD, who has repeatedly delivered his people.

verses.text: For the LORD will not forsake his people for his great name’s sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will not forsake his people for his great name’s sake, because it pleased him to make them his people. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to Israel as a nation and his gracious choice of them, which still leaves room for individuals and generations to fall under judgment, as 12:25 warns.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a strong statement of God’s electing commitment, grounded in his good pleasure and his name, not in Israel’s merit. Many connect it with Paul’s statement that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2). Both traditions agree that the verse grounds Israel’s hope in God’s character.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readers emphasize that God’s commitment is to Israel as a covenant people, which does not guarantee that every member or generation will escape the judgment of 12:25. Reformed readers emphasize that God’s purpose rests on his own good pleasure and name, so his commitment cannot finally fail, and they read the warnings as means of that faithfulness. Both agree the ground of hope is God’s character, not Israel’s merit.

verses.text: Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you; but I will instruct you in the good and the right way.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says that it would be sin against the LORD for him to stop praying for them, and he will teach them the good and right way. Arminians see faithful intercession and teaching as the duty of God’s servants, and they see prayerlessness named as sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see Samuel as a model of a pastoral leader who prays and teaches. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: intercession and instruction are means God uses to keep his people walking in his way.

verses.text: Only fear the LORD, and serve him in truth with all your heart; for consider what great things he has done for you.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel urges them only to fear the LORD and serve him in truth with all their heart, considering the great things he has done. Arminians see gratitude for God’s acts as the motive for faithful service, which they must choose to give.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that service is grounded in remembering God’s great things, so grace comes before obedience. Both traditions read the verse as the heart of Samuel’s address and as a summary of covenant faithfulness.

verses.text: But if you keep doing evil, you will be consumed, both you and your king.”
verses.arminianNotes: If they keep doing evil, both they and their king will be consumed. Arminians see the final warning as a real possibility that shows covenant blessing can be lost by persistent rebellion, as later happened in the exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the warning is real and was fulfilled in Israel’s later history. They read it alongside 12:22 as part of how God disciplines and preserves a people for his name. Both traditions see the address ending with a sober call to faithfulness.
